title: Work, Machines and Simple Machines
summary: The scientific meaning of work, what a machine does, the terms load, effort and pivot, and the difference between simple and compound machines.

p: In science, work is done when a force moves an object over a distance. Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force, and is measured in joules. If you push a wall and it does not move, you do no work on it in the scientific sense.

A machine is a device that makes work easier. It can do this in three ways: by reducing the effort needed (a lever); by changing the direction of the force (a pulley); and by increasing speed or distance moved (bicycle gears). A machine does not give you extra energy: the work you get out can never be more than the work you put in.
Load (L): the force or weight to be moved. Effort (E): the force you apply to the machine. Pivot (fulcrum): the fixed point about which a lever turns.

A simple machine has one or two moving parts and makes work easier. There are six kinds (see the next unit). A compound machine is made of two or more simple machines working together. Examples: a wheelbarrow (a lever and a wheel and axle), a bicycle (levers, wheels and axles, gears), a car, scissors (two levers and two wedges).

p: Mechanical advantage tells how many times a machine multiplies your effort: MA = Load ÷ Effort. It has no unit because it is a ratio of two forces.

Example: you lift a load of 100 N with an effort of 20 N. MA = 100 ÷ 20 = 5. The machine multiplies your effort by 5. You must however move the effort through a greater distance than the load moves, so you do not gain any work.

A single fixed pulley lifts a 50 N bucket of water with an effort of 50 N. MA = 50 ÷ 50 = 1. The pulley does not reduce the effort; it changes its direction, so you can pull down instead of lifting up.

Use a ruler as the lever and a pencil as the pivot. Place a heavy book (the load) near one end. Put the pencil under the 10 cm mark and push down on the other end to lift the book. Now move the pencil closer to the book. It becomes easier to lift, because the effort is now further from the pivot than the load is, so the MA is greater.

(a) A knife: a wedge (the blade). (b) A bottle opener: a lever. (c) A bicycle: a compound machine with levers (pedals, brake levers), wheels and axles, and gears. Two simple machines in the kitchen: a knife (wedge) and a tin opener (wheel and axle with a wedge), or a bottle opener (lever).

title: ICT and Scientific Advancement: Data and Analysis
summary: What ICT is, and how it has changed the way scientists collect, store and analyse data and run simulations.

p: ICT stands for Information and Communication Technology. It covers all the technologies used to store, process, find and share information: computers, smartphones, the Internet, software such as spreadsheets, email and satellites.

Before ICT, scientists wrote observations in a notebook, which was slow and limited. Now digital sensors (thermometers, weather stations, satellite scanners) collect huge amounts of data every second, day and night, called big data. The data is stored on powerful computers, hard drives or in the cloud (storage on servers reached through the Internet), where it is safe and can be reached from anywhere.

Before ICT, calculations were done by hand: slow and easy to get wrong. Now computers and software such as Excel can analyse millions of numbers in seconds and show patterns in charts. Scientists also run simulations: computer models used to test things that are too big, too small, too dangerous or too slow to test in real life, for example a car crash, climate change over 100 years or the spread of a virus.

NiMet uses satellites and weather stations to forecast weather for Nigerian farmers and airlines. Hospitals store patient records and scan results on computers. Researchers share data by email and video calls.

title: The Internet, Communication and Global Learning
summary: How the Internet connects scientists and learners around the world, and how to use it safely and well.

p: Before ICT, scientists sent letters that took weeks or months. Today a scientist in Nigeria can share data at once with a scientist in Japan by email, video conferencing or online research portals. This speeds up discovery.
Before ICT, a student relied on the books in the local library. With the Internet a student can find articles, videos, lectures and research papers from all over the world.

The Internet is a global network of computers. It is the most powerful ICT tool for science. It allows global collaboration (scientists on different continents worked together on the Human Genome Project); open access (many research papers are free online); and crowdsourcing (scientists ask the public to help, for example by reporting bird sightings or lending the spare power of home computers).

Check whether the website is reliable: look for the author, the date and other sources that agree. Do not share passwords or personal details. Do not believe every message you receive. Respect other people's work by giving credit and not copying.

Imagine you are a Nigerian scientist who finds a plant that might help to treat malaria. You would record your results carefully, store the data safely, write up your findings, send them by email to other researchers and publish them in a science journal online. You would also test the plant safely and have your results checked by other scientists before anyone uses it as a medicine.

title: Careers in Science and Technology
summary: The main career fields in medicine, engineering, ICT and research, and what each professional does.

p: These are jobs that need science, mathematics and technology to solve problems and create new things. They are among the most important jobs for building a modern country.

img.alt: Medical and research, engineering, ICT and programming, and agricultural science careers, linked by maths, problem solving and innovation
img.cap: STEM careers: medicine, engineering, ICT and agriculture.

p: Doctor: finds out what is wrong with a patient and treats illness and injury. Pharmacist: prepares and gives out medicines and is an expert on drugs. Medical laboratory scientist: tests blood, tissue and other fluids to help doctors diagnose disease. Nurse: cares for patients in hospitals and clinics. Radiographer: works the X-ray, CT and MRI scanners.

Civil engineer: designs and builds roads, bridges, dams and big buildings. Electrical engineer: designs electrical systems, power grids, electronics and computers. Mechanical engineer: designs machines such as engines, generators and cars. Chemical engineer: designs ways of turning raw materials into products, for example refining petroleum, making soap and processing food.

Software developer (programmer): writes the code for programs, apps and websites. Network administrator: runs and protects the computer network of a company or school. Data scientist: studies large amounts of data to find patterns and predict what may happen. Cybersecurity expert: protects computer systems from hackers and viruses.

Biologist or biotechnologist: studies living things and may develop new medicines or crops. Chemist: studies substances and may invent new materials such as plastics or batteries. Physicist: studies energy and matter and may work in space science or energy. Geologist: studies the Earth and looks for oil, gas and minerals. Agricultural scientist: improves crops, animals and farming methods.

title: Skills for Science Careers and Why They Matter to Nigeria
summary: The skills needed for careers in science and technology and how skilled professionals build the nation.

p: 1. A strong foundation in mathematics, physics, chemistry and biology. 2. Problem solving: the main job is finding answers to hard problems. 3. Analytical skills: looking at data and understanding what it means. 4. Creativity and curiosity: thinking of new ideas and asking 'Why?' 5. ICT skills: almost every science and technology job needs computer skills. 6. Teamwork and communication: most work is done in groups and results must be explained clearly.

A nation cannot develop without its own scientists, doctors and engineers. Health: more doctors and nurses mean a healthier, more productive population. Infrastructure: civil engineers build the roads and bridges that carry goods. The economy: ICT professionals and engineers start companies (for example the Nigerian financial technology companies Paystack and Flutterwave), create jobs and solve local problems. Self-reliance: with its own experts a country does not depend on others to build its infrastructure or solve its problems.

Pay special attention to mathematics and English, which are needed for almost every course at university. Join the science club and take part in science fairs. Read about people in your chosen career. Talk to a professional if you can. Choose your senior secondary subjects with your career in mind (for example biology and chemistry for medicine; physics and further mathematics for engineering).

title: The Scientific Method
summary: The steps of a science project from question to conclusion, with the idea of a fair test.

p: A science project is a hands-on investigation that uses the scientific method to answer a question or solve a problem. It is not just building a model; it is an experiment designed to find an answer.

1. Ask a question (problem). A bad question is a plain fact such as 'What is a plant?'. A good question can be tested: 'Does the colour of light change how fast a plant grows?' 2. Do background research: find out what is already known. 3. Form a hypothesis: an educated guess you can test, for example 'The plant under blue light will grow tallest.' 4. Design and carry out an experiment: plan a fair test. 5. Collect and record data in a table or chart. 6. Analyse the data: what do your results show? 7. Draw a conclusion: say whether your hypothesis was correct. 8. Present your findings. (Some books combine steps and count seven; the order is what matters.)

In a fair test you change only one thing, the independent variable (for example the colour of the light), and measure what happens, the dependent variable (the height of the plant). Everything else must be kept the same; these are the constants (the water, the soil, the type of plant, the temperature and the time). A control is a sample treated normally for comparison, for example a plant in ordinary light. Repeat the test several times to make the results reliable.

Question: Which brand of paper towel absorbs the most water? Hypothesis: Brand A will absorb the most. Method: take three brands; pour 20 ml of water into a dish; hold a sheet of Brand A in it for 10 seconds; measure the water that is left; repeat for B and C, and repeat each three times. Constants: the amount of water, the size of the sheet, the time and the dish. Independent variable: the brand. Dependent variable: the amount of water absorbed.

title: Planning, Teamwork and Presenting a Science Exhibition
summary: How to plan a project, share the work in a team, present at an exhibition and reflect on what you have learnt.

p: Planning is the most important step. Write down your question, your hypothesis, a list of the materials and the steps. Decide who will do what and by when. Think about safety.

Most projects are too big for one person. Divide the roles: one person does research, one collects materials, one takes measurements, one records data and one prepares the display. Listen to each other and share ideas to find the best solution. A good team respects every member.

A science exhibition is where you present your project. You usually need: a display board (a large folded card) showing title, question, hypothesis, method, data and conclusion; the experiment itself so that you can show it working; and an oral presentation of two to five minutes in which you explain what you did and what you found. Practise your talk, speak clearly and be ready for questions.
Projects are marked on the creativity of the question, correct use of the scientific method, the clarity of the data and results, and how well you present and explain the work.
Ask yourself: What went right? What went wrong? What would I do differently next time? Reflection turns experience into learning.

Which soil holds the most water? Does salt change how quickly ice melts? Which fruit peel keeps its colour longest? How much does a solar cooker raise the temperature of water? Which material is the best heat insulator for a cup?

title: Third Term Revision: Energy, Heat, Electricity, Machines and Science in Society
summary: A checklist of third term topics with key facts and revision practicals.

p: Energy: forms, transformations, conservation, potential and kinetic energy. Heat: conduction, convection, radiation, conductors and insulators, the vacuum flask. Electricity: sources, circuits and symbols, series and parallel, home wiring, safety, saving electricity. Science and development: science, technology, R&D, discovery, invention, innovation. Machines: work, the six simple machines, mechanical advantage. ICT: data, simulation, the Internet. Careers and skills. The scientific method and projects.

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. Conduction in solids, convection in fluids, radiation needs no medium. Homes are wired in parallel; the earth wire protects from shocks. MA = Load ÷ Effort. Science is knowing why; technology is applying it. A fair test changes one variable and keeps the others constant.
Trace the energy transformations in five devices. Identify the simple machines on a bicycle. Build a simple circuit and draw it. Design an experiment to answer one question of your own.
For 'trace the energy', write the forms in order with arrows. For circuits, use correct symbols and a ruler. For calculations, write the formula, substitute, then give the answer with its unit.
